STUDENT LOAN SCHEME AMENDMENT BILL (NO 3)
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I move, That the Student Loan
Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) be now read a third time . This bill continues the
Government’s efforts to ensure proper governance over the student loan scheme by
proposing tougher measures to deal with persistent non-payers and by raising the
repayment obligation of overseas-ba sed borrowers. Although the overwhelming
majority of borrowers accept the responsibility to repay their taxpayer-funded loan, the
reality is that some do not, despite having the financial ability to do so. The main
provision in the bill will allow the Inland Reve nue Department to seek an arrest warrant
to deal with the small group of mainly overseas-based borrowers. As I previously made
clear, this action would be taken only in the most serious of cases when the borrower
clearly has a financial ability to pay and when all other efforts to persuade that person to
make their repayments to the New Zealand taxpayer have failed.
The second major proposal in this bill raises the repayment obligation for overseas-
based borrowers to bring them more in line with their New Zealand-based counterparts.
Overseas borrowers with a loan balance over $45,000 will now have their repayment
16434 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
rates increased. This will speed up the repa yment rates for these borrowers and reduce
the amount of interest that they have to pay on their loans. These are the principal
features of the bill.
I want to acknowledge the work of those who have contributed to the successful
passage of this bill so far. Particularly, my thanks go to the policy officials and drafters
who have worked on the detail of this bill. I want to recognise members of the public
and representative groups who have made submissions on the proposed legislation and
have come before the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and the committee itself for
its recommendations to improve the transparen cy and cohesiveness of the student loan
scheme. Finally, I want to thank all those who will vote in favour of this bill, because
what this does is it sends a very clear message to those who have been afforded a very
good education—because the taxpayer has decided to provide them with loans that are
interest free in New Zealand, with interest when they go overseas—that they do have an
obligation to hard-working New Zealanders, New Zealand taxpayers, up and down this
country who have made this possible.
Finally, I must thank members of the Hous e for recognising the importance of these
measures and ensuring that the student loan scheme is managed efficiently and fairly.
The student loan scheme and the student loan debt book are in better shape than they
have been. They are certainly in better shape than when those opposite left the
Government benches and they are much, much better than they will be when—one day
in the future—they come back and ruin it again. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Well, that was a poor excuse for
a third reading speech from the member opposite, the Hon Todd McClay. He is
normally better than that. He really failed on the whole way through this bill, the
Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3), to give any good justification for the
gimmick, the tasteless gimmick, that is cont ained in this bill—the movement by that
party opposite to bring populist politics into the collection of debt for the student loan
scheme.
On this side of the House we support entirely the collection of student debt. Those
who have borrowed in order to get ahead, to better their own lot, to better the lot of their
families, we believe should repay the loans so that other generations can get ahead. This
Government takes quite a different view. It does not really pursue constructive options
to regain the debt. It does not. It washes its hands of it and then gives out these
gimmicks that cannot be enforced, and, if th ey can be enforced, they are tasteless and
likely to alienate young New Zealanders. Inst ead it is focused on restricting access to
education. This is the Government that is restricting access to education.
Let us not forget that the in terest-free loan scheme that we have in New Zealand was
introduced by the Clark Labour Government. We had an interest-bearing loan scheme
before that. Let us not forget also the many moves that Steven Joyce has taken to restrict
access to tertiary education. We on the Labour Party side of the House believe that
every New Zealander should have the opportunity to get ahead, should have the
opportunity to make the best of their talents, and, if they choose to pursue tertiary
education for their own benefit, for the benefit of their families, communities, wh ānau,
they ought to have that opportunity and they should not be restricted from studying on
the basis of not having enough money in their wallets or in their parents’ wallets to
pursue that education.
This Government now supports the intere st-free student loan scheme through gritted
teeth—gritted teeth. It has introduced administration charges because it could not return
interest to the loans without really facing a huge backlash. But the students of New
Zealand have woken up to it. The Government is not popular on campus. When I have
been to visit in Otago [ Interruption] there is a rising unpopularity among students as
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16435
they realise that this Government is restricting access to education more and more and
more.
I have an example of that. I hear an example is being called for, from the other side.
There is a 23 percent drop in the number of students claiming a student allowance in
Dunedin this year as compared with the previous year, which shows that the
Government’s policies are pricing New Zeal anders out of education. Postgraduate
students are no longer eligible to receive a student allowance, nor are students who are
studying towards a degree that takes over 200 weeks to complete. This constant
restriction to access to education is a pattern. This is a Government that wants to
preserve the interests of capital.
It is the same justification, the same  reason, for restrict ing representation on
university councils. This is the Government’s latest trick: converting university councils
from a representative body that produces good outcomes by virtue of having all the
stakeholders—the students, the unions, th e staff, the academics, and management
principles—represented around the board table to a cutback model that the universities
do not like, that the universities have spoken out against. And the question still lingers
in the air: if Steven Joyce really believes that 20 people around the board table make
ineffective decisions, what is he doing with that Cabinet structure?
Why is Steven Joyce making these decisions in the Cabinet structure, which he
hates? Why is he doing that? He is imposing on universities a system that they do not
want, which will produce less effective outcomes for New Zealanders. He is trying to
stamp down on access to education through any means possible, and that is an outrage.
It is an absolute outrage. We on this side of the House, the party of education, the
Labour Party, the party that believes in acce ss to education, interest-free student loans,
and the betterment of our society will not let that go unchallenged.

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: Well, in this bill you have to cos it’s not in there.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Ms Adams says “Well, you have to let it go cos we’re just
going to make it happen.” That is the kind of arrogant, out-of-touch Government that
we are seeing across the House. It is saying:  “We are going to roll this through and we
will not listen to any voices of criticism. We will charge interest when we like. We will
put gimmicks into law when we like. At the borders we will stop people who are
coming home to family funerals, and we will arrest them, and we will make an example
of them. We will alienate young New Zealanders because we are only interested in
preserving the interests of capital. We do not want just anybody showing up at the
university. We are going to clamp down on the management structures”—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Look, we are on a third
reading debate. If the member looks at Speaker’s ruling 122/4, it says: “Members must
confine themselves to the general principles of the bill as it emerged from the
committee.” I have given some latitude and I ask the member, in the time remaining, to
focus on the essence and the subject of what this bill is about.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: I will come back to the bill, but I would note that the
interjections opposite have inspired me to point out the hypocrisy from members across
the House as they promote this as a bill that encourages education, because they are
against that and there are no two ways about it.
The Tertiary Education Union said of this bill that it is “a poor alternative to making
education more affordable and accessible”. Those are the words of a submitter to the
Finance and Expenditure Committee, and the Minister of Revenue got up and had the
audacity to thank the submitters for making this bill easier to pass through the House.
They did not like it. They tried to tell the Minister that this bill does not help with access
to education, that there is a cheap gimmick in  it that is an attempt to popularise a voice
16436 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
against access to education, and this Government did not listen. The Minister has beans
in his ears. He did not want to hear those submitters who were critical of the bill.
The original intent of the student loan scheme was never to turn young New
Zealanders into exiled enemies of the State. But the bill is so very National Party. There
is no evidence at all that this bill will increase compliance, reduce loan balances, or any
such thing. It is simple authoritarian posturing, and I expect that students around New
Zealand and those who have student loan balances will see it for what it is. This
Government is a Government that is out of touch with the needs of New Zealanders. It
is out of touch with the aspirations of New Zealanders to better themselves through a
broader education, and that is why we have this measure in the bill that is designed to
further restrict access.
The measure is designed to keep some of our talent overseas, it seems, because they
will be fearful of coming home for a family wedding or a funeral. The police have said
in respect of this part of the legislation, the part that has the arrest at the border
provision, that they simply do not have the resources to implement it. So Mr Sabin
opposite, who was yelling before, might like to ask his mates in the police why they
said that, and why they directly criticised this aspect of the bill that we are debating
now. Why did his mates in the police say that the National Government has no idea—no
idea—whatsoever what it is asking for here, and that the police cannot implement this
bill? You would have thought they would have spoken to each other, but this is a
Government that is out of touch. It is a Government that is out of touch and not
interested in engaging even with those who would do the work of supporting it by
implementing the populist measures it is trying to introduce today.
We asked at the select committee, of cour se, for some estimates of how this would
change the lot of ordinary New Zealanders, what would happen at the border, whether it
could be implemented, how it would be implemented, and what measures would be
used. And there was nothing convincing that told  us that this bill would increase the
repayment of student loan balances. We heard from the submitters only the credible
answer that this will alienate young New Zealanders. This is a ridiculous measure, it
should not be in the bill, and the Government members are very quiet about it, it has to
be said. There was not much in the previous speech mentioning that measure, and they
are rightly—and they have gone quiet—embarrassed about this legislation.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: No, we’re not.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Mr Hayes, of course, is the only one who is not, and that is
typical because I think he has missed the poin t. Mr Hayes is not embarrassed by it, but
he is on his own over on that side of the House, and that is not an infrequent occurrence.
This is a Government that is going after the big end of town. Sorry, it is going out for
the interests of the big end of town. I wish it was going after the big end of town. It is
more interested in chasing one or two Ne w Zealanders coming through the border who
have a few thousand dollars outstanding but no means to repay it, and it is letting, in the
meantime, the likes of Google, Facebook, and others go completely unchallenged as
they do not declare for tax purposes the revenues coming out of New Zealand. We
know, for example, that Google declares for tax purposes only less than 5 percent of its
revenues out of New Zealand.
What is the Government across that side of the House doing about that? Absolutely
nothing—absolutely nothing. It is chasing a fe w students, saying “We’re going to arrest
you at the border if you come home.” That is an arrogant, out of touch Government that
is posturing ahead of the election and that has no idea about how it is actually going to
recoup the student loan balances. It is a Government that is out of touch and out of ideas
and should be sent packing at the next election. We need a Labour Government, the
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16437
kind of Government that is interested in broadening access to education and in giving
opportunities to all New Zealanders to better their lot for themselves and their families.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: The previous speaker, David Clark, obviously
came from the school that says that if you do not have a strong argument, shout. That
was his approach for that speech. It really surprises me because the Labour Party says
that it supports the general principle that loan borrowers should meet repayment
obligations for the money they have borrowed from the Crown. That is what it says. But
when it comes to it, Labour does not really want to do anything about it. The reality is
that we have a problem with default for people not paying back their loans when they
go overseas. We have 110,000 overseas borrowers at the moment, and 61,370 of them
are in default, with an amount outstanding of $543 million, and the total loan balance is
estimated to be around $3 billion.
That, according to the Labour Party, is not a problem, it is not an issue, and it is a
ridiculous thing to even try to get it back, whereas we here in the National Party take the
responsible view towards taxpayers and the people who have borrowed money from the
scheme. The responsible thing to do is to make sure that people pay their loans back.
The alternative, it seems to me, is to carry on doing nothing. So when we know that
somebody has a very large loan outstanding to fellow New Zealanders, we just say hello
to them at the airport, say “Thanks. Have a nice day.”, and do nothing about it. Well, we
are not going to do that any more, and this proposal is for only when every other
opportunity and avenue to encourage people to pay back their loans has been
exhausted—to have a final sanction in place. I think that that is absolutely appropriate
and very much in tune with the thoughts and needs of New Zealanders who want to
make sure that their money is spent wisely.
The Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) is part of National making the
student loan scheme sustainable into the future, because we know that we are not going
to get very far if we are not even conc erned about $543 million being owed to fellow
New Zealanders and we are not going to lift a finger about getting it back. It seems to be
a theme. There seems to be a theme in the Labour Party at the moment that you say one
thing and you do another. You thunder about trusts, and you have one of your own. You
thunder about the politics of envy in leafy suburbs, but you live in one yourself. You
say that you care about paying back loans, but when it comes to the crunch you do not
do anything about it—you do not do anything about it. So this debate is all about
making sure that the more than 100,000 overseas-based borrowers do their duty and pay
back those loans.
I just want to drill into one area here that we are talking about. The potential for
arrest at the border is a targeted measure aimed at those who consistently fail to meet
their responsibility to repay their loans. I do want to say that there were some
constructive comments during the select committee process, particularly from the New
Zealand First Party—not so much from the Labour Party, unfortunately, and the Greens
still seem to have a rather adolescent attitude to all this, which is that somehow we
should just throw the money at everybody and it is not a big deal if they do not pay back
the $543 million that is owed to fellow taxpayers. This bill is a responsible bill. It is
about bringing some discipline back to the scheme. We have been stepping away very
carefully, very cautiously, and sending a clear message that we expect people to pay
back their loans. I think that is fitting a nd appropriate, and on that basis I commend this
bill to the House.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: The Student Loan
Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) represents a disingenuous and confused Government
when it comes to the issue of student loans and student support. It is disingenuous
because, despite all the high-minded rhetoric about the importance of getting our loans
16438 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
paid back, the Government knows that doing this will affect very few loans. It will get
very, very little money back as a result of this bill, but it is waving a giant big stick
around that will have the effect of saying to many young New Zealanders overseas:
“Don’t come home. Don’t bother. We don’t want to see you. We don’t want your
contribution.” So, on the one hand, it is the big, proud Paul Goldsmith standing up and
saying “We’re not going to stand up for loan  defaulters.”, but, on the other hand, all
through the documentation the message is “We’re not really going to use it.” So, in
other words, it is disingenuous.
The Government is trying to look good. It is a gimmick. It is not a proper policy to
see student loans paid back. It is not a proper policy that talks to young New Zealanders
overseas and says: “Come back home and contribute to your country.” It is a
disingenuous gimmick from the National Government to look like it is being tough on
loan defaulters and to look like it is doing something about getting student loans paid
back, but in reality all it is doing is putting a gimmick in front of New Zealanders.
This is a Government that is out of t ouch with those New Zealanders overseas who
have that debt. I think that all members of Parliament will have received
communications from people affected by th is legislation. The overwhelming message
from young New Zealanders overseas to us in those communications is: “This is putting
me off coming home. This is making me say ‘Why should I come back to my
country?’.”
This Government, if it was really serious about getting student loan debt repaid,
would be looking at other sorts of arrangements, which we discussed in the Finance and
Expenditure Committee. For instance, we could have a repayment regime that is
actually about what people living overseas can afford to pay—not some arbitrary
measure that has been set in this bill, but, rather, an earnings-based assessment. We
were told by the officials: “Oh, that’s too difficult.” Well, it is not. For the vast majority
of people, they are living in countries where we have agreements that could facilitate
that, and we do. We are talking here about Australia and the United Kingdom. It is
actually perfectly possible to come up with a regime that is about what people can
afford to pay. One of the most common things we hear is that it is too complicated and
it is too much money, or it is not a realistic assessment of what someone is earning and
their outgoings overseas. A Government committed to getting repayments would
actually sit down and work out a regime where that could happen. But, instead, this
Government wants to come up with a policy that, frankly, as well as being
disingenuous, is unworkable.
At this point in the debate I would love to be able to refer to the pros and cons of this
idea from the regulatory impact statement. There were a variety of options proposed for
what could be done to increase repayments. The pros and cons for this particular one—
border restrictions—are not here. They are not  in the regulatory impact statement. They
have been withheld from it. So the National Government does not actually want us to
know what the arguments for and the arguments against this were. It just wants to come
to the House and say: “Agree with this gimmick. It will sound good. It sounds like
we’re doing something about it.” Well, that is simply not good enough.
It is not good enough to expect this House to agree to a provision that fundamentally
changes what has been a civil matter, the repayment of loans, and turns it into a criminal
matter. That is a serious change. If the National Government wants parties in this House
to support that, it should at least come with some evidence. It should at least come and
say “This is why we think this will work.” But, instead, the regulatory impact statement
is completely silent on the pros and cons—and, in particular, the cons—of this proposal.
That is because it is not really designed to work. It is actually designed as a gimmick.
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16439
What is in the paper, as it outlines this option, is the fact that it says—I will read you
a piece. Think about how this will work: “Once the borrower is located at the airport
Police would make a judgement as to whether to execute the arrest warrant or not. It is
important for Police to use their discretion and the decision to make an arrest may have
consequences for other passengers, the airl ine and airport security. It may not be
appropriate, for example, to arrest a single adult accompanying a young child if
adequate arrangements cannot be made for the child.” Oh well, maybe if we make
arrangements for the child, we will just go around and arrest people! This is ridiculous
policy. It sounds like a farcical situation. The police have told us quite clearly that they
do not have the resources to be sitting at the airport, trying to work out whether to arrest
people or not. It is a farcical policy and without proper justification.
What the Government could have done in this bill was talk about what it could do to
make the student loan scheme fairer. While this bill has been winding its way through
Parliament, the Government has made a number of changes to the student loan scheme
and the student allowance scheme. It ha s abolished postgraduate allowances. No
postgraduate student in New Zealand can now get an allowance. Along with a number
of other members of this House, I have been visiting university campuses over the
orientation period. I have been told, at our tw o largest universities, that there has been a
significant impact on the number of postgraduate enrolments.
For those people who can continue to do postgraduate study, there is a massive
increase in debt because they will have to use a student loan scheme that does not
adequately fund their living costs. In fact, a number of people, particularly
psychologists, architects, ophthalmologists, and those who have to do postgraduate
qualifications in order to practise, are leav ing, going overseas, because once again the

items.speaker: Government is saying
items.text: “There’s no reason to stay in New Zealand. We don’t value a
postgraduate qualification if you are not ri ch enough to be able to pay your way
yourself.” That is not good enough. So that happened while this bill was going through
the House.
Also what happened were the restrictions on access to loans and allowances based on
age. If you are over 55 years old, you cannot borrow living costs under the student loan
scheme, which limits the opportunities for people to retrain. If you are over 40, under
this National Government there are 3 years of entitlement for allowances through your
whole lifetime, and it is retrospectively applied as well. If you got 3 years of allowances
in your twenties, and you then worked but you lost your job, you then think: “I need to
retrain. I need to do something so I can contribute to the economy.” This National

items.speaker: Government says
items.text: “We don’t value you. You can’t have an allowance. You have to
apply for a loan, which you won’t be able to afford to live on.”

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: Not true. Not true. Telling porkies.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is true, Mr Hayes. Read your own policy, Mr Hayes.
There are no allowances if you are over 40 if you have already had 3 years of
allowances. But it goes on—it goes on. It used to be that when you came to New
Zealand as a new migrant you had to wait for 2 years before you could draw on the
student loan and support scheme. Now it is 3 years. I have had people in my office who
want to be in training and contributing to New Zealand. They have migrated to New
Zealand, and they want to start a life here, but they are not able to do that because of the
policy of this Government.
So while this bill has been going through the House access to the student loan and
allowance scheme has been cut back. The Government has introduced an administration
fee on the student loan scheme, because it wa s not brave enough to reintroduce interest
on student loans, which we know it wants to do. The Government has put on an
administration fee—another additional cost.
16440 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
We could have been having a conversation, on this Student Loan Scheme
Amendment Bill (No 3), about how we use the student loan scheme to get more people
into tertiary education and to give more people the opportunity to benefit themselves,
their communities, and their families. But, instead, we have a silly, gimmicky,
disingenuous policy that criminalises a whole lot of New Zealanders. It sends a message
to those New Zealanders overseas: “Don’t co me home. Don’t come back to contribute
to your country.” On this side of the House we believe this is a backward step. It is a
silly policy.
What we should be doing is saying to New Zealanders overseas: “There will be
opportunities for you.” I can assure those people who are overseas, and their families
here in New Zealand who are listening today,  that under a Labour-led Government we
will ensure that the student loan and allowance scheme actually works to encourage
people into education. Steven Joyce has said he wants to dampen demand for tertiary
education. I want to see enrolments increa se, qualifications increa se, and the tertiary
education system contributing to a positive future for all New Zealanders. Under this
Government it is a total failure. This bill is a ridiculous gimmick, and we will oppose it.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: The Green Party takes tertiary education seriously.
We see it primarily as a public good, and we consider that all New Zealanders benefit
from having a highly skilled and highly educated population. We think that tertiary
education should be affordable and accessible to all, and we think that every student,
including those aged over 40 and those doing postgraduate study, deserves access to
student support in the form of student loans and allowances. We think we need a
fundamental review and rewrite of the stud ent loan scheme, with the principles of
access and affordability at its heart. Sadly, this Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill
(No 3) is not that. In fact, it is one of a series of bills tinkering around the edges of the
student loan scheme, which is fundamentally broken and from which this National
Government is trying to wring every last dolla r, without looking at the bigger picture of
how we fund tertiary education and why we fund it. The Green Party in Government
would step back, and we would take stock of how we fund tertiary education and
student support to implement a better, smarter, fairer system that reflects the public
good inherent in an educated population.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: Why didn’t you bring it to the committee?

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: Because I was on maternity leave, Mr Hayes. It is time to stop
tinkering with the system and putting even more strain on the Inland Revenue
Department’s broken computer system with bills like this.
It is timely that this bill should come up this week, when thousands of students
around the country are heading for their first or  second week of lectures. Many of them
will not yet be thinking about how they are going to repay their student loans or whether
they are going to live in New Zealand or overseas after they graduate. They are
probably not aware that this bill will have a real impact on those decisions in the future.
This House has a tendency to deal in stereotypes, and the “lazy” student borrowing from
the “generous” student loan scheme to fund an education that will primarily deliver
them personal benefit in the form of high wages is one stereotype that we hear all the
time. National MPs like this stereotype because it means that they can pass punitive
little bills like this one without thinking too hard or feeling too bad about whom they are
affecting—never mind the fact that these so-called lazy students are the same ones
whom John Key was busy taking derp-faced Selfies with up at Victoria University
yesterday. I guess that they are good for just a laugh and a political photo opportunity,
but are not worthy of serious policy consideration.
But, actually, although this bill will impact the future decisions of current students,
the people it primarily affects right away are not current students, so the Government
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16441
MPs cannot hide behind that “lazy” stereotype  this time. The changes in this bill to
crack down on overseas borrowers by increa sing their repayment responsibilities and
allowing them to be arrested at the border—that is very disproportionate, right there—
will primarily affect graduates. Graduates do no t fit that stereotype of the lazy student.
They are people like the family who emailed me when the changes were announced in
last year’s Budget. This family lives in the United States so that the husband can pursue
his academic career. He earns US$41,000—a fairly moderate income. His wife is also a
PhD graduate. She is currently caring for their two small children. They both have
student loans in New Zealand, which they are fully committed to repaying. Because of
the changes in this bill, their minimum annual repayments will go up from $6,000 a year
to $9,000 a year, with no means testing and no accounting for the fact that only one of
them is in paid work and that they have two dependants. At the current rate of exchange
that means they will be paying approximately 19 percent of their income back towards
their student loan debts—19 percent of their income.
This family has a strong intention of returning to New Zealand. They fully intend to
repay their loans and they are currently compliant with all of their student loan
obligations. But these new payment obligations are totally unaffordable for this family,
and they cannot see a way to meet them that will not break their budget. If they default
on them because they simply cannot afford to meet their repayments, they now face
being arrested at the border if and when they re turn to New Zealand. Is this fair? Is this
proportionate? Is it a good use of time and resources to chase up families like this? Of
course it is not. But this is how this G overnment chooses to spend its legislative
resource.
I have lived and studied overseas and I can confirm that it is quite difficult to keep up
with student loan repayments while you are overseas. Information is hard to come by.
Making voluntary repayments is complicated. Communicating with the Inland Revenue
Department from overseas is difficult. Negot iating a repayment holiday or an interest
exemption is unnecessarily complicated. Many New Zealanders living or studying
overseas simply give up and resolve to deal with the problem when they return to New
Zealand. Should they give up? No. Should we ma ke it easier for people in this situation
to meet their repayment obligations? Absolutely we should. But is the way to do that to
whack them with non - means-tested repayment increases and arrest them at the border
if they fail to comply? Absolutely not. This bill actually makes it more difficult for
people in this situation to come home and sort out their student loans. That is what we
should be incentivising them to do. What it does is whack them with a massive
disincentive to ever come home because they will potentially face arrest and criminal
conviction.
It is madness, I would contend, for New Ze aland to be introducing laws and policies
that make it less likely for our tertiary graduates living overseas to come home when we
have huge numbers of New Zealanders leaving every year and not coming back. We
need policies that encourage them to come back to New Zealand and to stay in New
Zealand. In Government the Green Party would introduce a debt write-off scheme for
graduates to encourage them to stay and co ntribute in New Zealand, because the Green
Party would invest in their future. This bill is disproportionate. It is not likely to be
particularly effective, as we have heard from all of the advice that was given to the
Finance and Expenditure Committee. It creates yet more incentives for graduates like
this to never return to New Zealand. It is symptomatic of a Government that does not
value tertiary education as a public good, a Government that sees student support as a
political nuisance, and a Government that sees the student loan scheme and amendment
bills like this as opportunities to put the screws on graduates and squeeze more and
more students out of eligibility for student support. We have the opportunity in New
16442 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
Zealand to design a modern, smart, and fair tertiary student support system. The Green
Party in Government would grasp this opportunity with both hands and invest in our
future by investing in our students.

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: I rise to take a brief call on
the third reading of the Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3). This bill is about
sending a message that if you owe money you should pay it back. The student loan that
has been granted to students to enable them to continue and advance their tertiary
education is not a gift given by hard-working taxpayers in New Zealand; it is a loan, and
with that loan comes the reciprocal obligation that it is to be paid back.
We have heard that there is about $3 billi on owing by overseas-based borrowers, of
which there are about 100,000 borrowers, and, of those, quite a significant proportion,
61,000 borrowers, are not meeting their repayment obligations. That is money that is
owed by the students. They borrowed it fully aware that they had to pay it back. It is not
a gift, as I have said; they borrowed it from other New Zealand taxpayers. It is only
reasonable to send them that message and to expect them to pay it back. I do not believe
that it is disingenuous to expect repayment of a debt. I think that is being fair. I come
from the school of thought that says if you borrow money, that comes with obligations.
You pay it back.
What is wrong with expecting repayment of a debt? What is wrong with expecting
personal responsibility? We are not talkin g about lazy students. We are not talking
about them at all, as the previous speaker, Holly Walker, has just said. What we are
talking about is expecting them to comply with their loan obligations. It is as simple as
that: sending them a message. If you owe money, pay it back. This is a good bill. It
sends the right message. It is certainly not tinkering when we are talking about $3
billion of taxpayer money. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora. Unfortunately for Ms Wilkinson, her
numbers are somewhat inflated. The reason why there might be about $3 billion
outstanding at the moment is not that there is a large number of overseas-based
borrowers whose payments have been outstanding for a large period of time; it is that
there has been a large number of oversea s-based borrowers whose 3-year repayment
holiday has just finished. That has upped the numbers, as has the fact that the Inland
Revenue Department does not recognise these as overdue debts until they are 5 years
old. So, unfortunately, Ms Wilkinson might ha ve wanted to do a little bit more study
before she launched into that particular diatribe.
We have attempted to talk sense with the National Party over this issue. We have
attempted to get a win-win situation out of this bill, the Student Loan Scheme
Amendment Bill (No 3). We have attempted to get the National Party to see that it
makes better sense to stop a citizen on the way into your country, when they are on their
way in for a period of time, when they can provide you with a third party, when they
can organise to set up automatic payments, and when they can perhaps even borrow the
money from a family member and pay the debt, instead of arresting them on their way
out—instead of arresting your citizen on their way out.
I think Ms Wilkinson has done the country a favour. She has made it quite clear that
this is not about collecting debt; this is about sending a message. This is about sending a
message. And the only thing I can say to the New Zealand citizens who are out there
overseas, listening to the fact that Ms Wilkinson said that this Government is not
actually interested in your money, is that it wants to send a message by making an
example of you. It wants to arrest you at the border. It wants to pull you out of a line-up.
It wants to make an example of you in front of your peers, in front of other citizens, so
that other people will be afraid of their Government. There are many, many people
currently afraid of the National Government, but this is just another little niche in that
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16443
sort of a chain. All I can say to those overseas-based borrowers is if you get arrested at
the border, under this legislation, our website  address is nzfirst.org.nz. Give us a call.
Give us a call, because we are one of the only parties that will actually come down there
and will give you a hand.
I guarantee you that when a New Zealand c itizen is arrested at the border on their
way out, for at least one in five there will be an error from the Inland Revenue
Department. I will guarantee you that they will be disadvantaged by this Government
because it cannot see sense. I mean, we do not expect any common sense from the life
raft for this Government that is the ACT Party, but we certainly tried. We tried to talk
sense with the National Government. We tried to come up with a win-win situation, but
it would not have a bar of it. Now Ms Wilkinson has told us exactly why. It was not
about a win-win situation. It was not ab out clearing debt. It was about sending a
message. Well, thank you, Ms Wilkinson. Thank you very much. What about the
message that is being sent?
In the House earlier today we had the Minister of Women’s Affairs—I see she is still
here—sweating at question time because the Opposition asked her to list the things that
her department had done, that her Governme nt had done, to assist women to minimise
that pay equity gap. What this Government has done under recent legislation is take
away the ability of 40-year-olds to access higher education. And that goes directly to
women. It goes directly to the majority of women who go back in and take a second
chance at their education. This sort of policy goes directly to minimising that ability for
those women. So no wonder the poor Minister of Women’s Affairs was so inarticulate
at question time today, because we have not been able to find a common-sense answer
for that either, apart from sending another message to New Zealand women, which is:
“Don’t go into higher education. Don’t try to upskill yourself. Don’t try to minimise
that gender pay gap, because the National Government doesn’t like it.” So those are the
two messages we have had today from the National Government.
What about the ageism? What about the ageism on those aged 55 plus—the ageism
that says: “We’re not going to allow you to borrow for student allowances if you’re 55,
because we actually don’t believe in lifelong le arning. It is a little bit of a message we
put in our brochures, but we’re not really keen on it. It’s not a message we want to
send.”? Again, we have tried to have a conversation with the National Party. What is the
purpose of that? What is the purpose of that? We are going to have to make an
assumption because we cannot get a sensible answer out of the National Party. All we
can assume is that it is actually about the debt not being repaid. That is the message it
wants to send. We hate to think that the Government might put in some legislation to
arrest 55-year-olds or older if they do not pay back their student allowance.
It seems to us, again, nonsensical when we have laws in this country where let us say
the purpose is that if you are 55 or older and you have a student allowance debt, the
Government does not want you to actually be able to access that, just in case you die
with a debt. OK. Let us just say that that is its reasoning, because we cannot figure it out
and it will not tell us. We all know that in this country if you die with a debt, your estate
goes into probate. So any debt must be paid be fore any of the estate is then handed out
to anybody else. The Government has got a backup plan. We already have it in
legislation. If that person had a cent on th em, the Government would get it because
under probate there is a debt there.
Again, these are things that New Zealand First has tried again and again and again to
talk sense with this Government on. But this Government is ideologically directed along
this path of—there is a word I was going to use that would not be allowed in this House.
The Government is ideologically set on a path to do over its own citizens if it can save a
16444 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
buck. New Zealand First will strongly oppose this, and we strongly recommend that if
anybody gets arrested at the border, they call us. We will help you out.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: I have to say that I was at the Finance and
Expenditure Committee where all these discussions were held, and that lady from New
Zealand First who has just left the House now did not attend any of the discussions
about this legislation, the Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3), and made no
contribution. The New Zealand First representative at the select committee slept through
it—slept through it. They made no contribution at all.
I have listened with great interest to di scussions this afternoon. Our interest-free
student loan scheme is one of the most generous in the world and we want to keep it
that way. The student loan scheme represents a major financial commitment by
taxpayers, including from my electorate in the Wairarapa, to support people in tertiary
education. The Government wants to support st udents in tertiary education, but it is
important for students to take personal responsibility for repaying their loans. I agree
with Holly Walker that all of New Zealand has a stake in good tertiary education, but
loan borrowers need to keep their end of the deal and repay their loans promptly,
particularly people who take the money and skip overseas.
I do not agree with David Clark or Grant Ro bertson, who have spoken earlier today,
and who want to give taxes from hard-working people in my electorate in the Wairarapa
to people who will not pay their bills or meet their obligations. This country, I believe,
would be better governed by the first 60 people in the Eket āhuna phone book than by
any of the people in the Opposition who want to be elected later in this year to govern
this country. We will be far better governed by the first 60 names in the Eket āhuna
phone book than by any of the people in this Opposition. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call after that
sanctimonious lecture from someone about student loan schemes—someone who would
not have paid for his own tertiary education. As someone who did pay and borrow for
her tertiary education, it is something that I find quite offensive. What we have had is
the ongoing dribble from the opposite benches about how this is about personal
responsibility and if you borrow money, of course you have to pay it back—no
argument over here. We have said: “Yes, if people borrow money, they should pay it
back.” Our objection to the piece of legislati on that we have in front of us, the Student
Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3), is not only grounded in terms of equity and
fairness but about the fact that it is not going to work. I will come back to that a little bit
later.
We have been told that this is legislation that is going to send a message, and then we
get some kind of character from some kind of pantomime sitting in the corner of the
Government benches who just yells out “Communists!” from time to time whenever an
Opposition member is speaking. Well, we do not think it is communist to expect that we
have some kind of equality of access to tertiary education in this country. We think
there is a public good in that. We would not think it was too radical. But really what that
comedy character sitting in the corner over there is demonstrating is this Government’s
antipathy to people getting an education and to the fact that there should be tertiary
education that is accessible to a wide variety of New Zealanders, regardless of their
parents’ income.
This is entirely fitting with moves that the National Government has made right
throughout the time this bill has been before the House to restrict the number of New
Zealanders who can receive access to enter tertiary education. If you are aged over 40,
this Government has told you that you are too old and not worth investing in. It has no
idea of any kind of belief in lifelong learning  or the fact that people can retrain and they
will have some kind of value to New Zealand. No, this Government has deemed that
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16445
you are no longer worth investing in. That is it. If you have had your 3 years of student
allowance, you are over and out; you are not going to receive any more support from the
Government.
Over here on the Opposition benches, we think this bill is short-sighted and again
points to this Government’s rhetoric about its belief in transforming New Zealand. It
shows how arrogant and out of touch the Govern ment is that it thinks that New Zealand
can get ahead by restricting education and training for New Zealanders. Over here on
the Labour benches, we know that New Zealan d will be a better place if more people
can get into education and training. Our desire  is not to dampen the demand for tertiary
education, as is the self-declared aim of th e Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment—to keep people out of tertiary education. This is the same Minister who
talks a big game about science and innovation leading our economy. Well, he has also
cut postgraduates from having a student allowance. Way to go for an innovation-led
economy, to stop people doing wasteful thi ngs like postgraduate research! Who knows,
we may turn into an economy like one of those Scandinavian nations that values things
like research and that understands what that is worth to them as a country.
What I would like to see through the course  of this debate is one—just one—speaker
from the Government benches get up. We are now at the third reading of this piece of
legislation. I have sat in this House and listened to tired old drivel from the Government
benches about how this is about personal responsibility, about how this is sending a
message. Well, I would like to know how this piece of legislation is going to work.
When we believe they will work, Labour has supported the Government on measures to
make the repayment of student loans easier and to collect more of the student loan debt.
We have supported the Government on measures around making changes to the Inland
Revenue Department website—the fact that it would not be so difficult, that essentially
international bank transfers would have to occur in order for those living overseas to
meet their student loan obligations. We have supported them because we think they are
positive moves and they actually will make it easier for New Zealanders living overseas
to repay their student loans. But we will not support a gimmick that is not going to
work, that is unfair, and that criminalises what is a civil matter.
My colleague Grant Robertson read some bits from the regulatory impact
statement—the regulatory impact statement that comes before this House—that have
not been redacted, because the Government does not actually want us to know what the
options were. When it comes to options—other things that we consider—there is a
blank page. This is how much consideration this Government has given to what the real
options that might work are, and perhaps why we can only hear the speech notes being
regurgitated time and time again from the members opposite because they have nothing
of substance to say. This is just more ar rogant, out-of-touch legislation that is about
trying to look tough, when it is not going to achieve anything.
I would like to do a little bit of a reading—

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Oh, don’t bother. Just don’t bother.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: —from the regulatory impact statement, from where it comes
to how this is actually going to work in practice. Actually, the comedy character in the
corner is yelling out something other than “Communist!”. I wonder what it was.
This is how the legislation is going to work: “…Inland Revenue would request
information from airlines under section 17 of  the Tax Administration Act to determine
which flight a borrower is booked on. This information would be provided to Police
stationed at the airport who would have to locate the defaulter before they boarded their
flight.”—a good use of police resource—“Police have advised that as this would have to
be achieved without photos, often in large crowded areas, this could be difficult and
time consuming.” This is from the very organisation that is supposed to be the body that
16446 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014
implements these crazy, lunatic gimmicks that the Government is proposing. The police
are telling them it is not going to work. But, yet again, Government members will stand
up and they will dutifully read from their arrogant and out-of-touch speech notes that
this is about sending a message and about us getting tough on defaulters, when all the
time they are narrowing the number of New Zealanders who will receive the benefit of a
tertiary education in this country.
This is a Government that will consider it a success if it can deny more and more
New Zealanders access to a university, a polytech, or any form of training. This is not
something that we think is in any way beneficial to New Zealand. We think that
regardless of your ability to pay to go and learn a trade or go to university, or your
family’s ability to pay for you, if you have the talent, you should be able to do that. I
have not heard one piece of evidence from the members opposite. I challenge the next
Government speaker to depart from their speech notes with the tired old lines and to
actually tell us how it is going to work, because the police have told us that it is not. I
would like to know how it is that this legislation is going to work.
The original intent of the student loan scheme was to make access to education
available to more New Zealanders. That is what we in Labour will cling dearly to. We
will not in any way support the Government’s move to narrow access to education. If it
really did want to get real about reducing the debt that defaulting student loan borrowers
owe to New Zealand and to the New Zealand taxpayer, then it would have looked at
some things that could have worked. It would have looked at measures about entering
into repayment arrangements with people. When Labour was in Government and we put
in place such a scheme, there was a huge surge in the number of people who went on
repayment plans, started paying their loans, and were no longer defaulters on their
loans. The Government has the evidence—a good field trial—of what actually did
work, but instead it is resorting to fanciful gimmicks that sounded good on Budget day
to try to appeal to its base, rather than something that will actually tackle this problem.
This is not the way that we are going to build a better New Zealand. This is not the
way that we are going to have an economy that is fit for the 21st century and based on us
having a highly skilled, highly educated workforce, and not excluding large numbers of
New Zealanders from that. Not only do the individuals suffer but we as a country will
suffer from this Government’s close-minded views on tertiary education.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That was a shocking speech on
the Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) from the Opposition by Dr Megan
Woods, but it just goes to reflect the nature of its argument here today. There are more
people in tertiary education under this Government than under the previous
Government. That is because we have opened access up. Opposition members are not
telling the truth in this House tonight by saying that there has been a restriction on
education. It is far from the truth. The real truth is that the Labour Party does not want
people to pay their debts. What gives the Labour Party, the Green Party, and New
Zealand First Party the mandate to go out there and say that you can go to a New
Zealand educational institution, you can get New Zealand training, and then you can go
overseas and get a free ride, whereas if you stay in New Zealand and you make this
country stronger, you have to repay your debt? Under the policy of the Labour Party,
the Green Party, and the New Zealand First Party, why do we give an exemption from
paying their debt back to those people who leave this country? Why do they want to do
that?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: We don’t.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: They do. That is what they are saying, because they do not
want those people to repay their debts—that is the simple truth of it. Do you know why?
It is the socialist elite over there who believe that they have a right to some higher
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16447
position in New Zealand’s soci al hierarchy, and who believe that they should get a free
education and not have to pay it back. That socialist elite that is the Labour Party has
never represented the people whom they try to stand for. The people out there working
in factories who pay for those educational institutions—what do they get? They get to
see some other young person—who is in the socialist elite—go overseas and not repay
their debt. What about those people who actually go and get training in New Zealand
and then work in New Zealand? They have to pay it back. But under the Labour Party,
if you go overseas you get an exemption.  This is disgusting to see from Labour, the
Greens, and New Zealand First: that New Zealanders are treated differently if they
leave. That is what they are saying, and that is not good policy. We want New
Zealanders to pay off their loans and pay their debt back.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Andrew Little—five minutes.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to have the opportunity to talk about
student loans once again. It is the first time in about 20 years, I might add, and I had a
lot to say then, usually at the end of a megaphone in the front of this great building, or
on the streets of Wellington.
The point is that this bill, the Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3), is about
enacting the same powers for our Inland Revenue Department as the Russian tax
department has for its tax de faulters. We know how it treats its tax defaulters. Its
equivalent of our Inland Revenue Department turn up in full camouflage gear, fully
blacked out, armed with AK-47s, tommy knockers, and all the rest of it, and they go
smashing down and smashing people up when they do not pay their taxes.
This is a bill that is completely over the top when it comes to enforcing the
obligations of student loan defaulters. The student loan scheme was introduced, and has
been in place in various forms, to enable people to get access to education. It is
unfortunate that over the last 20 or 30 years the state of the economy, for whatever
reason, has been such that the State cannot afford access to education for those who
need it and who are capable of taking it up.  We have moved to more of a user-pays
system, and so the student loan scheme has come in to facilitate that. But we need to
make sure that we do not introduce a mechanism and a scheme that becomes so punitive
and ugly in its implementation that it puts people off.
There are a number of reasons, as previous speakers in this House have alluded to,
why those who have taken out student loans and gone out into the great wide world
once they have completed their studies—which is something that we encourage young
New Zealanders to do—can find it difficult to commence or recommence their student
loan repayments. The last thing we need is to have in place a scheme that intimidates,
bullies, and conjures up fear for New Zealanders when they are overseas, encouraging
them not to return.
You know what we most want in this country? We want educated young people. For
those who undertake a form of tertiary education and are required to take out a loan in
order to get access to it—whether it is education in our tertiary institutions, in the trades,
or in any other form of training—we do not want to create a disincentive for them to use
those skills and deploy themselves in a way th at is for the benefit of New Zealand. That
is what this bill will do. That is why we ar e so fiercely opposed to it—it is just not good
for the long-term interests of young New Zealanders who take up the opportunity of
tertiary education, or for New Zealand itself when it comes to harnessing the skills, the
learning, and the talents that they have developed. That is why this bill is so wrong.
All the National Party members opposite have left to fall back on is the tired old
rhetoric about irresponsible young people—

items.speaker: Simon OConnor
items.text: This is ironic as well.
16448 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 6 Mar 2014

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: And here is the irresponsible young Mr O’Connor—the
youngest old fogey of them all—who sits ther e bleating out the tired old rhetoric of the
tired old fogies of the National Party, saying: “We don’t want irresponsible youth.”
Well, it is not about that. It is actually about our brightest and best who, because of
everything else the National Government has done, race off overseas because that is the
best they can do for themselves. We want to make sure that the conditions are right for
them to come back. They know that when the next Labour-led Government comes in in
a few months’ time, they will be flooding back, because that is when they will see
opportunity.
We do not want a law on the books that tells them that when it is time for them to
come back, if they have not been able to repay their loans for reasons beyond their
control, they are going to be harassed and harangued at the border, clapped in
handcuffs, and frogmarched off to the nearest prison before they can enjoy their
freedom. We do not want that. That is not what a responsible education system does,
that is not what a responsible inland revenue system does, and that is not what a
responsible piece of legislation does when it comes to enforcing student loans, but this
bill is the opposite of that.
This bill is irresponsible, it is nasty, and it is petty—everything that the National
Party is characterised by and stands for. Nastiness and pettiness are reflected in this bill,
and that is why we are opposed to it. We are in favour of education, we are in favour of
responsible students, and we are in favour of  responsible lending. That is why we will
oppose this bill.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: This has been sort of quite a big week for tertiary
education. There have been a number of key announcements, and here, at the end of the
sitting week, at least, we are debating this dreadful bill, the Student Loan Scheme
Amendment Bill (No 3), which is being foisted on our young people and, indeed, on
anyone who participates in tertiary educati on. We have seen this week, of course, the
launch of a very deeply flawed tertiary  education strategy, which seems to have
emerged from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment rather than the
Ministry of Education, focused as it is on economic outcomes. The references to
education are almost incidental, which is a very sad reflection on the priorities and the
sheer lack of understanding of the value of education that we have seen emanating from
this Government over the past several years.
We have seen the changes to the Perfo rmance-based Research Fund. There are,
again, one or two good shifts, but primarily they are a great big leap backwards to the
extent that the objective that sought to ensure a fair distribution of the funding across
institutions and across disciplines has been  removed. In future, that funding will
advantage those who already have ready access  to external forms of funding, which is
perverse when you think it through. Researc h that is readily commercialised, for
example, and that therefore has ready access to external funding sources will be
privileged over social research and other forms of research where there is no obvious
external donor or beneficiary. It is a very backwards-looking change that has emerged.
Now, of course, we come to this bill, which is probably at least as backwards as any
of the other events of this week. This legislation undoubtedly does provide yet another
layer of disincentives to people participatin g in tertiary education in New Zealand. We
have heard the phrase “dampen down demand”. Clearly, this Government is very
interested in rationing. The Greens and, I believe, our Labour colleagues believe that
tertiary education based on merit is a right embedded in international and national
covenants. Those who are able and who aspire to such things should have the
opportunity to achieve at tertiary-level education. This Government would see it as a
6 Mar 2014 Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) 16449
privilege, something that is limited and rationed to the lucky few who have the
wherewithal to pay their way as they go.
The disincentives are clear. We will criminalise people who, for whatever reason, are
unable to keep up with their student loans. Our colleague from New Zealand First,
Tracey Martin, made the very good point that we can confidently expect that there will
be people whose travel plans are seriously compromised in error. I will not bore you
again with the stories, but I am sure others have similar ones. I have mentioned them in
previous speeches on this topic, like my own experience of getting two different
statements, two different letters, on the same day about the state of my student loan with
entirely different numbers on them. Those mistakes will continue. Nothing is surer.
Although I do not know where my colleague from New Zealand First got the statistic of
one in five, it sounds about right intuitively. We will penalise people who have
maintained their payments simply through errors in the bureaucracy of what is a very
complex system.
We are criminalising people. Absolutely, if people borrow money, they ought to pay
it back. That is a given. We probably are too thoughtless in terms of allowing young
people to get themselves heavily indebted, but, again, for many of them there is no other
option. The fact that the repayment model will not be income related is blindingly
stupid. Assuming that all of our young gr aduates who go overseas immediately walk
into highly paid jobs is a nonsense. That is not the reality for most of them.
As Holly Walker said before, the Greens see the public good element as well as the
private benefit. We heard bellowing from the National benches earlier asking who pays.
Well, yes, tertiary education has to be paid  for. For a long time we had a very robust
system where we paid for it primarily through the taxation system rather than through
loading debt on young people at the point in their lives when they have got the least
capacity to generate income. Let us do th is through our progressive taxation system,
where we claw it back once people get into well-paid positions. Yes, I am perfectly
happy then for people, through their taxes, to be paying for the education system—
primary, tertiary, secondary, across the board. It is immoral, almost, to load debt on to
young people at the point in their lives when they are least likely to be able to pay it
back and then criminalise them for that failure. Thank you.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Contrary to the assertion of Mr
Clendon, the Student Loan Scheme Amendment Bill (No 3) is not dreadful, but the
quality of the contributions to this debate from members opposite certainly has been.
This is not an immoral measure; this is a responsible and fair one. We have been far
from relying on rhetoric and ideology on this side, as members opposite have suggested.
That has entirely characterised the contributions from those members, and it is clear that
they are burying their heads in the sand. This bill is fair to all parties. This bill is in the
interests of the country, definitely in the interests of the New Zealand taxpayer, and
ultimately in the interests of the students themselves. I support this bill.
